newsitem.title: UK: British Labour party to shun Euro in 1999 - paper.
newsitem.headline: British Labour party to shun Euro in 1999 - paper.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party is moving towards a decision to stay out of the first wave of a European Union single currency if it goes ahead in 1999, the Times newspaper said in its Thursday edition.

The Times, itself often hostile to a single currency, said that privately the party's "most influential figures" were voicing serious doubts over whether a Labour government, if it came into power next year, would want to make such a move so soon after taking up office.

Labour's current stance is to seek voters' approval either through a referendum or a general election but the Times said opinion at the top of the party was hardening in favour of the decision being delayed, possibly until the election after next.
Britain's ruling Conservative Party, which is split over whether to join a single currency, must call a general election by May 1997.

The Times said senior Labour figures believe Britain's EU partners would not regard the party's approach as anti-European because they would understand that after nearly 18 years out of power, Labour was not ready to make up its mind.

One reason some commentators have started to talk about Labour's approach to the single currency is that its foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook told the party's conference that jobs would be "the bottom line" for European economic and monetary union entry, interpreted by some as a hardening of the its position.
In an interview on Wednesday Labour leader Tony Blair stressed EMU would have to take place on the basis of genuine convergence or Europe would face severe economic problems.
He drew a parallel with Britain's experience when it was forced to leave the Exchange Rate Mechanism and said it was important to ensure that similar problems on a wider scale wre not repeated.

But asked by BBC television whether he was signalling that Britain under a Labour government would not be among the first wave of countries to join a single currency, Blair replied: "I'm not saying never to a single currency."
He repeated Labour's existing policy that it would take the decision when the time came based on its judgement of Britain's national interest.
